epithet: Asad Allah al-Ghalib (Lion of Allah the Victorious); Amir al-Mu'minin (during his caliphate)
role: Cousin and Son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ
summary: Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) was the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, one of the earliest Muslims, and the fourth of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. He was raised in the household of the Prophet ﷺ from a young age, and his life spans the full arc of early Islamic history — from the first moments of revelation to the turbulent first fitna. He is celebrated for his courage in battle, his profound knowledge of Islamic sciences, and his deep spiritual character.
biography:
Ali ibn Abi Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib al-Hashimi al-Qurashi was born around 601 CE in Makkah, into the Banu Hashim clan — the clan of the Prophet ﷺ himself. His father was Abu Talib, the Prophet's uncle and guardian after the death of Abd al-Muttalib. When Abu Talib faced financial difficulties in caring for his large family, the Prophet ﷺ and his uncle al-Abbas each took one of his sons to raise in their homes. Ali was raised by the Prophet ﷺ, becoming effectively a member of his household from early childhood. This intimate proximity to the Prophet ﷺ shaped Ali's character and knowledge in ways that made him unique among the Sahaba.

Ali accepted Islam as a child — the majority of scholars, including Ibn Sa'd, al-Dhahabi, and Ibn Kathir, hold that he was the first youth (boy who had not yet reached puberty) to accept Islam, having believed immediately when the Prophet ﷺ called him privately. The exact age is debated: he was likely between nine and thirteen years old at the time. Regardless of ranking disputes, his Islam predates essentially all of the adult companions, and he lived in the Prophet's household throughout the Makkan period.

During the night of the Hijrah (1 AH / 622 CE), Ali demonstrated extraordinary courage. The Quraysh had plotted to assassinate the Prophet ﷺ by sending forty men from different clans so that Banu Hashim could not seek collective retaliation. The Prophet ﷺ instructed Ali to sleep in his bed, wearing his green cloak, to deceive the plotters while the Prophet slipped away under divine protection. Ali agreed and lay in the Prophet's bed through the night, fully aware of the potential danger. He then remained in Makkah for three days to return the trusts that people had left with the Prophet ﷺ before following to Madinah. (Ibn Hisham, al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn Sa'd)

The Prophet ﷺ gave him his daughter Fatimah al-Zahra (RA) in marriage in the second year of the Hijrah — a union of singular significance in Islamic history. Together they had Hasan, Husayn, Zaynab, and Umm Kulthum. Through Hasan and Husayn, all who claim descent from the Prophet ﷺ (the Sayyids and Sharifs) trace their lineage. The Prophet ﷺ referred to Fatimah, Ali, Hasan, and Husayn collectively in hadith of great significance; they are sometimes referred to in classical scholarship as the Ahl al-Kisa (people of the cloak).

Ali's bravery in battle was legendary throughout the Muslim world. He bore the banner for the Muslims at numerous battles and was among the foremost warriors at Badr, Uhud, and Khaybar. At the Battle of Khaybar (7 AH), when the fortress could not be taken for several days, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love. Allah will grant victory through him.' The next morning he gave it to Ali. (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Jihad; Sahih Muslim, Kitab Fada'il al-Sahaba). Ali single-handedly defeated the fortress's champion, Marhab al-Khaybar, and was instrumental in the conquest. His sword, Dhul-Fiqar, became one of the most celebrated symbols in Islamic military tradition.

Ali's knowledge of the Quran and Sunnah was among the deepest of the Sahaba. He had memorized the Quran in full and is credited with extraordinary jurisprudential acuity. Umar ibn al-Khattab frequently sought his counsel in complex legal matters, saying on multiple occasions: 'Were it not for Ali, Umar would have been ruined.' Numerous complex fiqh questions resolved during Umar's and Uthman's caliphates involved Ali's input. He also served as the scribe of certain letters for the Prophet ﷺ.

After the murder of Uthman ibn Affan (35 AH / 656 CE), Ali accepted the caliphate amid extreme turbulence. His era was defined not by external expansion but by internal trials — the first fitna (civil war) of the Muslim community. Three major confrontations occurred during his caliphate: the Battle of the Camel (36 AH / 656 CE) against forces supporting Aisha, Talhah, and al-Zubayr, which began over demands for justice in Uthman's murder; the Battle of Siffin (37 AH / 657 CE) against Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, who also demanded justice for Uthman; and the Battle of Nahrawan (38 AH / 658 CE) against the Khawarij — those who had initially fought alongside Ali but then declared him an apostate for accepting arbitration after Siffin.

Classical Sunni scholarship — and this is the position of Ibn Taymiyyah in Minhaj al-Sunnah al-Nabawiyyah, al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', and Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah — holds that all parties in these disputes were Muslims acting on their own ijtihad (legal reasoning). None of the Sahaba involved are condemned as sinners, apostates, or evildoers, though classical scholars generally hold that Ali (RA) was on the correct side as the legitimate Caliph. These events are presented neutrally, as the classical scholars did, while acknowledging that the full truth of these complex situations belongs to the judgment of Allah alone.

Ali was martyred in 40 AH (661 CE) by Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite, who struck him with a poisoned sword while he was performing the Fajr prayer in Kufah. He died two days later at the age of approximately sixty years, having been Caliph for roughly four years and nine months. He was buried in Kufah (the city of Najaf in present-day Iraq is the traditional burial site, though some classical scholars noted uncertainty about the exact location).

The Prophet ﷺ said of Ali: 'You are to me as Harun was to Musa, except there is no prophet after me.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). He also said: 'I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate.' (Recorded with varying chains; al-Hakim graded it sahih in al-Mustadrak; subject of scholarly debate on chain, but referenced by many classical scholars including al-Suyuti). His rank among the Sahaba, his courage, his knowledge, and his profound love for the Prophet ﷺ place him among the greatest figures of the first generation of Islam.

key_events.event: Born in Makkah; raised in the Prophet's household from an early age
Accepted Islam as a young boy — the first youth to embrace the faith
Slept in the Prophet's bed the night of the Hijrah to deceive the Quraysh plotters
Married Fatimah al-Zahra bint Muhammad ﷺ
Fought at the Battle of Badr — one of the foremost warriors
Led the assault at the Battle of Khaybar; given the banner by the Prophet ﷺ
Accepted the caliphate following Uthman ibn Affan's murder
Battle of the Camel near Basrah
Battle of Siffin against Mu'awiyah; arbitration accepted at Adhruh
Battle of Nahrawan — defeated the Khawarij
Assassinated in Kufah by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam while performing Fajr prayer

notable_traits: Unparalleled physical courage and martial skill — among the greatest warriors in Islamic history
Profound knowledge of Quran, hadith, and jurisprudence
Raised in the Prophet's household — extraordinary proximity to the source of revelation
Forebearer of all prophetic lineage through his sons Hasan and Husayn
Known for eloquence — attributed speeches and sayings collected in Nahj al-Balaghah (verified partially; scholars exercise care in attribution)

key_relationships.father: Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib (uncle of the Prophet ﷺ)
spouses: Fatimah al-Zahra bint Muhammad ﷺ (his first and most significant marriage)
After Fatimah's death: Umamah bint Abi al-As, Khawlah bint Ja'far, Umm al-Banin bint Hizam, Layla bint Mas'ud, and others
key_relationships.prophetic_connection: Cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ; from Ahl al-Bayt
